profile.campus: Miami, Miami-Dade County, Florida (Equinix MI1, NAP of the Americas)
profile.reading:
Per the Wikipedia article on the NAP of the Americas, this Miami, Florida building sits at 50 NE 9th Street in downtown Miami and totals 750,000 square feet across 6 stories, described as one of the worlds largest data centers. Now operated by Equinix (as MI1) after Equinix acquired the building from Terremark Worldwide (a Verizon subsidiary) in 2016 for 3.6 billion dollars as part of a 24 data center portfolio deal. The building sits 32 feet above sea level and is engineered for Category 5 hurricane conditions, hosts 160 network carriers, provides peering to AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, and connects to 15 subsea cable landings plus a K-root DNS server. The article does not state a power capacity in MW.

Equinix's acquisition of the building came as part of a broader 2016-2017 deal in which Equinix acquired 24 data centers from Verizon (including the Terremark portfolio) for roughly 3.6 billion dollars, one of the largest transactions in Equinix's history and the deal that brought the NAP of the Americas, marketed today as Equinix MI1, into the company's Americas colocation network. The building functions as a major hub for Latin American and Caribbean connectivity given Miami's position as a subsea cable landing point, and its hurricane-category-5 engineering and elevated siting reflect its role as critical infrastructure for a hurricane-prone metro. Equinix's current MI1 property page (added as a second source alongside the Wikipedia entry) confirms the building remains an active, named facility within Equinix's Miami-metro colocation portfolio, though it does not itself disclose current occupied sqft or MW figures separate from the Wikipedia-sourced 750,000 sq ft total.

Miami-Dade County's data center market has grown substantially since Equinix's 2016-2017 acquisition of this building, with the county now hosting one of the densest concentrations of subsea cable landing stations in the Western Hemisphere; the NAP of the Americas name persists in industry and local usage even though Equinix has marketed the building as MI1 since taking ownership, and it remains one of the largest single data center buildings by square footage documented anywhere in this registry.

reading.body:
NAP of the Americas is a 750,000-square-foot facility in downtown Miami that connects to AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, plus 15 subsea cables and 160 network carriers, making it a critical internet exchange point rather than a compute center itself.

The facility functions as infrastructure for infrastructure. It hosts peering agreements and DNS routing rather than the GPUs and processors that run AI workloads. Its value to AI companies lies in the connectivity it provides: low-latency access to cloud providers, subsea cable landings that reach international markets, and K-root DNS which handles domain lookups for roughly one-seventh of the internet. These are prerequisites for compute to function at scale, not substitutes for it.

The building sits 32 feet above sea level in hurricane country, engineered for Category 5 conditions. This reflects a real constraint: data centers require both power and cooling, and coastal facilities that host subsea cables risk storm damage. The facility's defensibility against hurricanes matters for continuous operation of the peering and routing services that AI infrastructure depends on. However, the data does not include the building's power capacity or consumption, so it cannot show whether power is a binding constraint here or how much capacity this location absorbs from the Miami grid.
